grid.statement: fd.mesh.rectangle_mesh(nx=11, ny=11, x_min=0, x_max=1, y_min=0, y_max=1, elm_type='quad4', ndim=None, name='') creates a rectangular Mesh; nx, ny are the numbers of nodes in the x and y axes (default 11) and x_min/x_max/y_min/y_max the boundary of the rectangle (default 0, 1, 0, 1)
elm_type accepts 'tri3', 'tri6', 'quad4', 'quad8', 'quad9' (default 'quad4'); for 'quad9' and 'tri6' the function forces nx and ny to odd values (nx = nx // 2 * 2 + 1, same for ny)
The function returns the generated geometry as a fedoo Mesh object (class fedoo.core.mesh.Mesh)

Related mesh builders in the same module: line_mesh (1D line mesh, def at line 330), box_mesh (3D volume mesh, def at line 478), grid_mesh_cylindric and line_mesh_cylindric (cylindrical), as listed in the docstring 'See Also'

grid.statement: fd.weakform.StressEquilibrium(constitutivelaw, incompressibility=None, convert_tangent=True, name='', nlgeom=None, space=None) is the mechanical equilibrium equation for solids, usable for a solid in 3D or using a 2D plane assumption (plane strain or plane stress)

nlgeom: set to False if geometric nonlinearities are ignored; True or 'UL' activates geometric nonlinearities based on the updated Lagrangian method (update the mesh); 'TL' uses the total Lagrangian method (based on the initial mesh with initial displacement effect); if not defined, the problem.nlgeom parameter is used instead (used in the context of NonLinearStatic or NonLinearNewmark problems)

The weak form accepts geometric nonlinearities only if simcoon is installed (nlgeom in {True, 'UL', 'TL'}); in that case the initial displacement is also considered and several corotational formulations may be used by setting the corate attribute (default 'log_r', other options 'log', 'jaumann', 'green_naghdi'/'gn', ...)
For nearly incompressible materials, the incompressibility attribute selects a method to avoid the volumetric locking; by default (None) the standard displacement formulation is used

grid.statement: FKN is real constant R3, the 'normal penalty stiffness factor'; the penalty method (KEYOPT(2) = 1) uses the real constants FKN and FKT for all values of KEYOPT(10), plus FTOLN and SLTO if KEYOPT(10) = 0 or 2

FKN defines a normal contact stiffness factor; the usual factor range is from 0.1 to 10.0, with a default of 1.0 (Section 3.9.4.2); a negative value for FKN defines an absolute normal contact stiffness
FKN APDL default is 1 (range 0.1-10.0, section 3.9.4.2)

For FKN (and FTOLN, PINB, PZER, CZER, FKOP, FKT, SLTO, TNOP, FDMN, FDMT) the program interprets a positive value as a scaling factor and a negative value as the absolute value; contact-related settings (FTOLN, PINB, FKN, FKT, SLTO) are always averaged across all contact elements in a contact pair

grid.statement: fd.ModelingSpace(dimension, name='Main') creates the space in which coordinates and variables (functions over coordinates) are defined; a modeling space is required to be able to define weak equations
dimension must be one of '2D', '3D', '2Dplane', '2Dstress', '2Daxi'; the string '2D' is mapped to '2Dplane'

'2D'/'2Dplane' = general 2D problems with default coordinates 'X' and 'Y' and plane strain assumption (ndim=2); '3D' = 3D problems with coordinates 'X', 'Y', 'Z' (ndim=3); '2Dstress' = same as 2D but with plane stress assumption; '2Daxi' = same as 2D but with axisymmetric assumption

A newly created ModelingSpace automatically becomes the active space and is stored in the class dictionary under its name (retrievable as fd.ModelingSpace['Main']); the active space can be changed with make_active() or set_active(name) and read with get_active()

grid.statement: NLGEOM,ON activates large-deflection effects; select Large Displacement Static when large deflections are expected (e.g. a long, slender bar under bending)
LNSRCH activates the line search option (listed in the Nonlinear tab options of Solution Controls)
PRED activates a predictor on the degree-of-freedom solution; NEQIT specifies the maximum number of equilibrium iterations allowed per substep
CNVTOL sets the convergence criteria; CUTCONTROL controls bisections (cutback criteria)

NROPT (Newton-Raphson option) is used only in a nonlinear analysis and specifies how often the tangent matrix is updated: Program-chosen (default), Full, Modified, Initial stiffness, Full with unsymmetric matrix
AUTOTS enables automatic time stepping; DELTIM and NSUBST control the time step size / number of substeps (TIME sets time at end of load step)

dFacts.statement: NLGEOM,OFF ignores large-deflection effects (a small-deflection analysis is specified); this option is the default.
dFacts.note: Lines 52003-52005: 'OFF / Ignores large-deflection effects (that is, a small-deflection analysis is specified). This option is the default.' Cited line is within the statement span.

dFacts.statement: NLGEOM,ON includes large-deflection (large rotation) effects or large strain effects, according to the element type.
dFacts.note: Lines 52006-52008: 'ON / Includes large-deflection (large rotation) effects or large strain effects, according to the element type.' Adds large-strain/element-type detail beyond G1, so not a duplicate.

dFacts.statement: When large-deflection effects are included (NLGEOM,ON), stress stiffening effects are also included automatically, and the command is valid only within the first load step during the solution.
dFacts.note: Lines 52014-52016: stress stiffening included automatically when NLGEOM,ON (52014-52015); 'If used during the solution (/SOLU), this command is valid only within the first load step.' (52016). Cited line is in-span.

dFacts.note: Line 52017 verbatim: 'In a large-deflection analysis, pressure loads behave differently than other load types.'

dFacts.statement: NCNV KSTOP: 0 = do not terminate the analysis if the solution fails to converge; 1 = terminate the analysis and program execution (default); 2 = terminate the analysis but not program execution.

Predictions for nonlinear element status change... Size of the plastic strain increment... Size of the creep strain increment.' Cited line verbatim the anchor.

dFacts.statement: The automatic solution convergence check uses the L2-norm of force (and moment) with TOLER equal to 0.5%, and in most cases an infinite norm check on displacement with TOLER 5% is also used as a double-check.
dFacts.note: Cited line 13911 is the preceding sentence. True support at lines 13912-13916: 'The automatic solution convergence check uses the L2-norm of force (and moment) with a tolerance (TOLER) equal to 0.5%... an infinite norm check on displacement with TOLER equal to 5% is also used... serves as a double-check on convergence.'

dFacts.statement: By default, the program checks force convergence by comparing the SRSS of the force imbalances against VALUE*TOLER, where VALUE defaults to the SRSS of applied loads or MINREF (which defaults to 0.01), whichever is greater.
dFacts.note: Lines 13917-13920 verbatim (SRSS of force imbalances against VALUE*TOLER; VALUE default SRSS of applied loads or MINREF (defaults to 0.01), whichever is greater). Cited line in-span.

dFacts.statement: You should continue to use the default value of VALUE, changing convergence criteria by adjusting TOLER not VALUE, and ensure the default MINREF = 0.01 makes sense.
dFacts.note: Cited line 13928 is the preceding sentence. True support at lines 13930-13932: 'you should continue to use the default value of VALUE; that is, change the convergence criteria by adjusting TOLER, not VALUE. You should make certain that the default value of MINREF = 0.01 makes sense in the context of your analysis.'

dFacts.statement: The infinite norm repeats the single-DOF check at each DOF; the L1 norm compares against the sum of absolute values; the L2 norm uses SRSS; normally convergence in one norm implies convergence in the others.
dFacts.note: Lines 13937-13950: infinite norm 13937-13938, L1 norm 13944-13945, L2 norm (SRSS) 13946-13947, 'Normally, if an analysis converges in one norm, it will converge in the other norms' 13949-13950. Cited line is the span start.

dFacts.statement: Automatic solution control sets NEQIT to between 15 and 26 iterations; if convergence is not satisfied within this number and auto time-stepping is on, the program attempts to bisect, or terminates/moves on according to NCNV.
dFacts.note: Cited line 13944 is the L1-norm bullet. True support at lines 13952-13959: 'Automatic solution control sets the value of NEQIT to between 15 and 26 iterations... the program attempts to bisect. If bisection is not possible, then the analysis either terminates or moves on to the next load step (according to NCNV command settings).'

dFacts.statement: Automatic solution control activates a predictor (PRED,ON); the linear extrapolation is based on the previous time step's accumulated displacement increment, the quadratic on the previous two, and quadratic predicts better for rotational DOFs (ROTX, ROTY, ROTZ).
dFacts.note: Lines 13961-13974: 'Automatic solution control activates a predicator (PRED,ON)' (13961); linear extrapolation on previous time step's accumulated displacement increment, quadratic on previous + prior-to-previous (13966-13970); 'quadratic extrapolation typically predicts better... for solutions with rotational degrees of freedom (ROTX, ROTY, ROTZ)' (13972-13974). Cited line is inside the supporting span.

dFacts.statement: Automatic solution control toggles line search on and off as needed: LNSRCH is toggled on for most contact problems and off for most non-contact problems.
dFacts.note: Lines 13979-13980 verbatim: 'Automatic solution control toggles line search on and off as needed. For most contact problems, LNSRCH is toggled on. For most non-contact problems, LNSRCH is toggled off.'

dFacts.statement: The line search multiplies the calculated displacement increment by a scale factor between 0 and 1 when stiffening is detected; it is an alternative to adaptive descent (NROPT), and activating both simultaneously is not recommended.
dFacts.note: Cited line 13983 is a copyright page-break line inside the paragraph. True support at lines 13981-13990: 'multiplies the calculated displacement increment by a program-calculated scale factor (having a value between 0 and 1), whenever a stiffening response is detected... alternative to the adaptive descent option (NROPT)... We do not recommend activating both line search and adaptive descent simultaneously.'

dFacts.statement: When an imposed displacement exists, a run cannot converge until at least one iteration has a line search value of 1, and the program does not impose the full displacement until then.
dFacts.note: Lines 13991-13995 verbatim: 'When an imposed displacement exists, a run cannot converge until at least one of the iterations has a line search value of 1... Until one of the iterations has a line search value of 1, the program does not impose the full value of the displacement.'

dFacts.statement: CUTCONTROL provides finer control over bisections and cutback in time-step size; by default for Lab=PLSLIMIT, Value is set to 15 percent.
dFacts.note: Lines 13997-13999: 'For finer control over bisections and cutback in time-step size, use (CUTCONTROL, Lab, Value, Option). By default, for Lab = PLSLIMIT (maximum plastic strain increment limit), Value is set to 15 percent.' Cited line in-span; adds the 15% default beyond G4.

dFacts.statement: Automatic solution control uses the FULL Newton-Raphson option (NROPT) with adaptive descent off if a nonlinearity is present, but turns adaptive descent on automatically for node-to-node/node-to-surface contact with friction.
dFacts.note: Lines 14023-14031: 'Automatic solution control uses the FULL Newton-Raphson option (NROPT) with adaptive descent off if there is a nonlinearity present. However, when node-to-node, node-to-surface contact elements are used for contact analysis with friction, then adaptive descent is automatically turned on.' Cited line in-span.

dFacts.statement: NROPT,FULL updates the stiffness matrix at every equilibrium iteration; with adaptive descent on, the program discards divergent iterations and restarts using a weighted combination of secant and tangent matrices.
dFacts.note: Lines 14036-14044: 'Full (NROPT,FULL): The program uses the full Newton-Raphson procedure, in which the stiffness matrix is updated at every equilibrium iteration... If divergent trends are detected on an iteration, the program discards the divergent iteration and restarts the solution, using a weighted combination of the secant and tangent stiffness matrices.' Cited line is the anchor bullet.

dFacts.statement: NROPT,MODI updates the tangent stiffness matrix at each substep and is not applicable to large-deformation analyses; NROPT,INIT uses the initial stiffness matrix and is also not applicable to large-deformation analyses.
dFacts.note: Lines 14049-14057: MODI 'tangent stiffness matrix is updated at each substep... not applicable to large-deformation analyses'; INIT 'uses the initial stiffness matrix in every equilibrium iteration... not applicable to large-deformation analyses'. Cited line is the anchor bullet; adds not-applicable-to-large-deformation detail beyond G5.

dFacts.statement: You should first try NROPT,FULL, then try NROPT,UNSYM if you experience convergence difficulties; a multistatus element is updated at the iteration in which it changes status irrespective of the Newton-Raphson option.
dFacts.note: Cited line 14070 is a copyright line. True support at lines 14075-14079: 'You should first try NROPT,FULL, then try NROPT,UNSYM if you experience convergence difficulties... If a multistatus element is in the model, it is updated at the iteration in which it changes status, irrespective of the Newton-Raphson option.'

dFacts.statement: To account for buckling/bifurcation behavior, the program includes stress stiffness in all geometrically nonlinear analyses (NLGEOM,ON).
dFacts.note: Lines 14020-14021 verbatim: 'To account for buckling, bifurcation behavior, the program includes stress stiffness in all geometrically nonlinear analyses (NLGEOM,ON).'

dFacts.statement: Bisection provides a means of automatically recovering from a convergence failure by cutting a time-step size in half when equilibrium iterations fail to converge and restarting from the last converged substep.
dFacts.note: Lines 12984-12986 verbatim: 'Bisection provides a means of automatically recovering from a convergence failure. This feature cuts a time-step size in half whenever equilibrium iterations fail to converge and automatically restart from the last converged substep.'

dFacts.statement: In a large-deflection analysis, nodal coordinate system orientations are not updated and calculated displacements are output in the original directions; pressure loads always act normal to the deflected element surface.
dFacts.note: Lines 13003-13004: 'Nodal coordinate system orientations are not updated in a large deflection analysis. Calculated displacements are therefore output in the original directions.'; lines 12999-13000: 'Pressure loads always act normal to the deflected element surface'. Cited line in-span.

dFacts.statement: Large-strain analyses account for stiffness changes from changes in an element's shape and orientation; NLGEOM,ON activates large-strain effects and the procedure places no theoretical limit on total rotation or strain.
dFacts.note: Lines 13046-13047: 'large-strain analyses account for the stiffness changes that result from changes in an element's shape and orientation. NLGEOM,ON... activates large-strain effects...'; lines 13050-13051: 'The large-strain procedure places no theoretical limit on the total rotation or strain experienced by an element.' Cited line in-span. (Source has minor typo 'NLGEOM,ON), activates large-strain effects supported element types' â€” readable, not a defect.)

dFacts.note: Cited line 13050 is the no-theoretical-limit sentence. True support at lines 13052-13053: 'The procedure requires that strain increments be restricted to maintain accuracy, however, so the total load should be broken into smaller steps.'

dFacts.note: Lines 13055-13056 verbatim: 'In large-strain solutions, all stress-strain input and results are in terms of true stress and true (or logarithmic) strain.' Cited line in-span.

dFacts.note: Cited line 13092 is the initial-stress sentence. True support at lines 13093-13094 verbatim: 'For most elements, initial stiffness effects are automatically included when large-deformation effects are activated (NLGEOM,ON).'

dFacts.statement: A structure can become unstable when a load reaches its buckling value or when nonlinear material becomes unstable; it is more common in slender structures, and the instability could be global (snap-through of a plate) or local (failure of a stiffener).
dFacts.note: Lines 14609-14611 verbatim (8.11 Unstable Structures). Cited line is the span start.

dFacts.statement: Nonlinear stabilization (p. 303) is a tool for dealing with local instabilities as well as global instability and can be used with nearly any other nonlinear technique (such as line search and automatic time-stepping) but not with the arc-length method.
dFacts.note: Lines 14615-14618: 'Nonlinear stabilization (p. 303) / A tool for dealing with local instabilities as well as global instability. You can use it together with nearly any other nonlinear solution technique, such as line search and automatic time-stepping (although not with the arc-length method).' Cited line in-span.

dFacts.statement: The arc-length method (p. 308) can simulate the negative slope portion of a load-vs-displacement curve.
dFacts.note: Lines 14619-14621: 'Arc-length method (p. 308) / This method can circumvent global instability... More importantly, it can simulate the negative slope portion of a load-vs.-displacement curve.' Cited line in-span.

dFacts.statement: The energy dissipation ratio should be between 0 and 1; use a smaller value for local instability and a larger value for global instability, a smaller value for solid elements and a larger value for shell, beam, and link elements.
dFacts.note: Line 14687 verbatim ('The energy dissipation ratio should be between 0 and 1...'); guidance at lines 14695-14699: 'use a smaller value for local instability and a larger value for global instability. The smaller value should be used for solid elements and the larger value should be used for shell, beam, and link elements.' within +30.

dFacts.statement: It is more efficient and accurate in most cases to activate stabilization in a multiframe restart, restarting from the next-to-last converged substep.
dFacts.note: Lines 14825-14826: 'it is more efficient and accurate in most cases to activate stabilization in a multiframe restart'; lines 14827-14829: 'do not restart from the last converged substep. Rather, restart from the next-to-last converged substep...'. Cited line in-span.

dFacts.statement: If the stabilization energy is much less than the potential energy (for example, within a 1.0 percent tolerance), the result should be acceptable.
dFacts.note: Lines 14802-14804 verbatim: 'If the stabilization energy... is much less than the potential energy (for example, within a 1.0 percent tolerance), the result should be acceptable...'. Cited line in-span.

dFacts.statement: The arc-length method (ARCLEN and ARCTRM) is restricted to static analyses with proportional (ramped) loads only; do not use LNSRCH, PRED, adaptive descent (NROPT,,,ON), automatic time-stepping (AUTOTS, DELTIM), or TIMINT when it is active.
dFacts.note: Lines 14869-14870 verbatim ('restricted to static analyses with proportional (ramped) loads only'); lines 14877-14880: 'do not use line search (LNSRCH), the predictor (PRED), adaptive descent (NROPT,,,ON), automatic time-stepping (AUTOTS, DELTIM), or time-integration effects (TIMINT)' within +30. Cited line is the span start.

dFacts.statement: When the arc-length method is active, do not base convergence on displacement (CNVTOL,U); instead use the force criteria (CNVTOL,F).
dFacts.note: Cited line 14878 is the preceding sentence. True support at lines 14879-14880: 'Likewise, do not try to base convergence on displacement (CNVTOL,U); instead, use the force criteria (CNVTOL,F).'

dFacts.statement: If an arc-length solution fails to converge within NEQIT, the program automatically bisects and continues; you can freely switch from Newton-Raphson to arc-length at the start of any load step, but switching from arc-length to Newton-Raphson requires terminating and restarting with ARCLEN,OFF.
dFacts.note: Lines 14881-14884: 'If an arc-length solution fails to converge within the prescribed maximum number of iterations (NEQIT), the program automatically bisects and continues the analysis'; lines 14893-14896: 'You can freely switch from the Newton-Raphson iteration method to the arc-length method at the start of any load step. However, to switch from arc-length to Newton-Raphson iterations, you must terminate the analysis and restart... (ARCLEN,OFF).' Cited line in-span of first clause; second clause within +30.

dFacts.statement: Place an upper limit on the time-step size (DELTIM or NSUBST), especially for complicated models, to ensure all modes and behaviors of interest are accurately included.
dFacts.note: Lines 15194-15196 verbatim (8.12.2.4 Automatic Time-Stepping). Cited line is the span start.

dFacts.statement: Line search (LNSRCH) is useful for enhancing convergence but expensive (especially with plasticity); consider it for force-loaded structures, 'flimsy' structures with increasing stiffness (such as a fishing pole), and oscillatory convergence patterns.
dFacts.note: Lines 15219-15224 verbatim (8.12.2.5 Line Search) including the three bullets (force-loaded, flimsy/fishing pole, oscillatory convergence). Cited line is the span start.

dFacts.statement: The nonlinear stabilization method can be used to solve both locally and globally unstable problems and to overcome convergence for general problems.
dFacts.note: Lines 15226-15228 verbatim (8.12.2.6 Nonlinear Stabilization). Cited line is the span start.

dFacts.statement: The Graphical Solution Tracking (GST) feature displays the computed convergence norms and criteria while the solution is in process; by default GST is ON for interactive sessions and OFF for batch runs, controlled by the /GST command.

By default, GST is ON for interactive sessions and OFF for batch runs. Use the /GST command to turn GST on or off.' Cited line is the span start.

dFacts.statement: Issue the NLDIAG,NRRE command to write Newton-Raphson residuals from equilibrium iterations to a file (Jobname.nrxxx), which can be contour-plotted via PLNSOL,NRRE.
dFacts.note: Lines 15119-15121 verbatim: 'Issue the NLDIAG,NRRE command to write the Newton-Raphson residuals from equilibrium iterations to a file (Jobname.nrxxx). You can then contour plot the residual forces via the PLNSOL,NRRE command...'.

dFacts.statement: The nonlinear example (8.14) activates geometric nonlinearity with nlgeom,on and monitors displacement (monitor,1,ntop,uy) and reaction force (monitor,2,nright,fy) with outres,all,all.

dFacts.note: Lines 1718-1719 verified verbatim, but this is a strict subset of G5 ('NROPT... is used only in a nonlinear analysis and specifies how often the tangent matrix is updated: ...'). No new content.

dFacts.statement: In the TIME option, time acts as a tracking parameter in rate-independent analyses; if TIME is not issued, the program uses the default time value of 1.0 for the first load step and 1.0 + previous time for other load steps.

dFacts.statement: For a nonlinear or transient analysis, specify the number of substeps within a load step via the DELTIM and NSUBST commands; by default the program uses one substep per load step.
dFacts.note: Lines 3416-3419 verbatim (3.6.1.2), including 'By default, the program uses one substep per load step.' Cited line is the span start.

In automatic time stepping, the program calculates an optimum time step at the end of each substep, based on the response of the structure or component to the applied loads. When used in a nonlinear static (or steady-state) analysis, AUTOTS determine the size of load increments between substeps.' Cited line is the anchor.

dFacts.statement: KBC,0 indicates ramped loads and KBC,1 indicates stepped loads; the default depends on the discipline and type of analysis.
dFacts.note: Lines 3427-3428 verbatim (3.6.1.4): 'KBC,0 indicates ramped loads, and KBC,1 indicates stepped loads. The default depends on the discipline and type of analysis.' Cited line in-span.

dFacts.statement: Table 3.14 lists NEQIT (maximum number of equilibrium iterations per substep), CNVTOL (convergence tolerances), and NCNV (options for terminating analyses) for nonlinear analyses.

dFacts.statement: Convergence is assumed when the residual (out-of-balance) is less than a tolerance times a reference value and/or the DOF increment is less than a tolerance times a reference value; the default is out-of-balance convergence checking only.
dFacts.note: Lines 30053-30055 verbatim (14.10.2 Convergence): 'Convergence, therefore, is obtained when the size of the residual (disequilibrium) is less than a tolerance times a reference value and/or when the size of the DOF increment is less than a tolerance times a reference value. The default is to use out-of-balance convergence checking only.'

dFacts.statement: The default out-of-balance reference value Rref is ||{Fa}||; for DOFs with imposed displacement constraints, the default Rref is {Fnr} at those DOFs.
dFacts.note: Lines 30079-30080 verbatim: 'The default out-of-balance reference value Rref is ||{Fa}||. For DOFs with imposed displacement constraints, the default Rref value is {Fnr} at those DOFs.'

dFacts.statement: There are three available norms (CNVTOL NORM): infinite norm, L1 norm, and L2 norm (SRSS); the default is to use the L2 norm.

grid.statement: KEYOPT(2) on the contact element selects the contact algorithm: 1 = penalty method, 0 = augmented Lagrangian (default), 3 = Lagrange multiplier on contact normal + penalty on tangent, 4 = pure Lagrange multiplier, 2 = internal multipoint constraint (MPC)

The penalty method uses a contact spring whose stiffness is the contact stiffness; it uses real constants FKN (normal contact stiffness factor) and FKT (tangent contact stiffness factor), plus FTOLN and SLTO if KEYOPT(10) = 0 or 2

The augmented Lagrangian method (default) is an iterative series of penalty methods; contact tractions are augmented during equilibrium iterations so final penetration is smaller than the allowable tolerance (FTOLN); it leads to better conditioning and is less sensitive to contact stiffness magnitude but may need more iterations with distorted meshes

The pure Lagrange multiplier method enforces zero penetration when closed and zero slip when sticking; it does not require FKN/FKT but requires chattering control parameters FTOLN and TNOP; it adds contact tractions as additional DOFs and often increases computational cost

FTOLN is the thickness-based factor used to calculate allowable penetration; SLTO controls maximum sliding distance when MU (friction coefficient) is nonzero; PZER defines pressure at zero penetration; CZER defines initial clearance

Lagrange multiplier methods (KEYOPT(2) = 3, 4) introduce zero diagonal terms in the stiffness matrix, so iterative solvers (e.g. PCG) encounter a preconditioning matrix singularity - switch to the sparse solver; also not compatible with Gauss point detection (KEYOPT(4) = 0)

dFacts.note: Lines 1815-1816 exact (CONTA172 2D 3-node higher order parabolic, SHELL208/PLANE183).

dFacts.statement: CONTA174 is a 3D, 8-node, higher order quadrilateral element that can be located on the surfaces of 3D solid or shell elements with or without midside nodes (e.g., SHELL181, SHELL281) and can be degenerated to 3- to 7-node shapes.

dFacts.statement: TARGE170 is used to represent various 3D target surfaces for the associated contact elements CONTA174, CONTA175, and CONTA177; for rigid targets these elements model complex shapes and for flexible targets they overlay the solid, shell, or line elements describing the deformable body boundary.

dFacts.statement: Asymmetric contact is defined as having all contact elements on one surface and all target elements on the other (one-pass contact) and is usually the most efficient; symmetric (two-pass) contact designates each surface as both target and contact and is used e.g. when the distinction is not clear or both surfaces have very coarse meshes.
dFacts.note: Lines 1485-1500 exact: one-pass usually most efficient; two-pass used when distinction unclear or both surfaces very coarse.

dFacts.statement: For each symmetric contact definition there are two contact pairs (base and companion); by default KEYOPT(8)=0 activates both pairs, KEYOPT(8)=1 activates both with the same averaged characteristics, and KEYOPT(8)=2/3 let the program internally select which asymmetric pair to activate.
dFacts.note: KEYOPT(8) list at lines 34501-34514: 0=both pairs active, 1=both active same characteristics, 2/3=program selects asymmetric pair. Note: ERef says "symmetric pairs"/"companion pair" (KSYM, line 35014); "base pair" wording and "averaged" qualifier come from CTG SS3.5.1.2 (line 1503) and are not stated in ERef.

dFacts.statement: For surface-to-surface contact elements the available algorithms are: Penalty (KEYOPT(2)=1), Augmented Lagrangian (default, KEYOPT(2)=0), Lagrange multiplier on contact normal and penalty on tangent (KEYOPT(2)=3), Pure Lagrange multiplier (KEYOPT(2)=4), and Internal MPC (KEYOPT(2)=2).
dFacts.note: Same claim as G1 (KEYOPT(2) value-to-algorithm mapping incl. defaults); verified at CTG 3060-3064 but excluded as duplicate of original grid fact G1.

dFacts.statement: The penalty method uses a contact spring (contact stiffness) and uses real constants FKN and FKT for all values of KEYOPT(10), plus FTOLN and SLTO if KEYOPT(10)=0 or 2.
dFacts.note: Same claim as G2 (penalty uses contact spring, FKN/FKT for all KEYOPT(10), +FTOLN/SLTO if KEYOPT(10)=0 or 2); verified at CTG 3065-3067 but excluded as duplicate of G2.

dFacts.statement: The augmented Lagrangian method (default) is an iterative series of penalty methods that augments contact tractions so final penetration is smaller than the allowable tolerance (FTOLN); it usually leads to better conditioning and is less sensitive to contact stiffness magnitude but may require additional iterations if the mesh becomes too distorted.
dFacts.note: Same claim as G3 (AugLag iterative penalty series, tractions augmented, final penetration < FTOLN, better conditioning, less stiffness-sensitive, more iterations with distorted mesh); verified at CTG 3068-3074 but excluded as duplicate of G3.

dFacts.statement: The pure Lagrange multiplier method enforces zero penetration when contact is closed and zero slip when sticking, does not require FKN and FKT but requires chattering control parameters FTOLN and TNOP, adds contact traction as additional DOF, and often increases computational cost.
dFacts.note: Same claim as G4 (pure LM: zero penetration/zero slip, no FKN/FKT, needs FTOLN+TNOP, extra DOF, higher cost); verified at CTG 3075-3080 but excluded as duplicate of G4.

dFacts.statement: The Lagrange multiplier on contact normal / penalty on tangent algorithm enforces zero penetration and allows a small amount of slip for sticking; it requires chattering control parameters FTOLN and TNOP as well as the maximum allowable elastic slip parameter SLTO.
dFacts.note: Statement at lines 3081-3084 (cited line 3085 is the following MPC sentence): LM on normal + penalty on tangent, zero penetration, small slip, needs FTOLN+TNOP+SLTO.

dFacts.statement: The internal multipoint constraint (MPC) algorithm is used in conjunction with bonded contact (KEYOPT(12)=5 or 6) and no separation contact (KEYOPT(12)=4) to model several types of contact assemblies and kinematic constraints.
dFacts.note: Statement at lines 3085-3088 (cited line 3093 is the following LM-considerations item): MPC with bonded (KEYOPT(12)=5 or 6) and no separation (KEYOPT(12)=4).

dFacts.statement: The Lagrange multiplier methods (KEYOPT(2)=3,4) do not support the Gauss point detection option (KEYOPT(4)=0) for surface-to-surface contact.
dFacts.note: G6 already states "also not compatible with Gauss point detection (KEYOPT(4) = 0)"; verified at CTG 3091-3092 but excluded as duplicate of G6.

dFacts.statement: The Lagrange multiplier methods introduce more degrees of freedom which may result in spurious modes for modal and linear eigenvalue buckling analyses, so the augmented Lagrangian method (KEYOPT(2)=0) is a better choice for these analysis types.
dFacts.note: Statement at lines 3112-3114 (cited line 3103 is off): extra DOF -> spurious modes for modal/linear eigenvalue buckling; AugLag (KEYOPT(2)=0) better choice.

dFacts.statement: The Lagrange multiplier methods introduce zero diagonal terms in the stiffness matrix, so iterative solvers (e.g., PCG) encounter a preconditioning matrix singularity; switch to the sparse solver.
dFacts.note: G6 already states zero diagonal terms -> PCG preconditioning singularity -> sparse solver; verified at CTG 3115-3117 but excluded as duplicate of G6.

dFacts.statement: Four different contact algorithms are implemented in CONTA174 (selected by KEYOPT(2)): pure penalty, augmented Lagrangian (Simo and Laursen), pure Lagrange multiplier (Bathe), and Lagrange multiplier on contact normal and penalty on frictional direction.
dFacts.note: Lines 21991-21995 exact: four algorithms selected by KEYOPT(2) (pure penalty, AugLag Simo & Laursen, pure LM Bathe, LM on normal + penalty on frictional direction). Distinct from G1 (which lists the 5 KEYOPT(2) options incl. MPC).

dFacts.statement: The pure penalty method requires both contact normal and tangential stiffness; the main drawback is that the amount of penetration depends on this stiffness, and higher stiffness values decrease penetration but can lead to ill-conditioning of the global stiffness matrix and convergence difficulties.
dFacts.note: Lines 21997-22000 exact: penalty requires normal+tangential stiffness; penetration depends on stiffness; high stiffness -> ill-conditioning/convergence difficulties.

dFacts.statement: The contact pressure for the pure penalty method is P = Kn*un (Equation 13.240), where Kn is the contact normal stiffness and un is the contact gap size; the frictional stress for isotropic friction is obtained by Coulomb's law (Equation 13.241) where Ks is the tangential contact stiffness (input as FKT on the R command) and Î¼iso is the coefficient of friction.
dFacts.note: Lines 22014-22027: Eq 13.240 contact pressure with Kn=contact normal stiffness, un=contact gap; Eq 13.241 Coulomb friction with Ks=FKT (R command), mu_iso. Equation bodies missing in PDF extraction (image equations) but variable definitions fully support the claim.

dFacts.statement: The augmented Lagrangian method is an iterative series of penalty updates to find the Lagrange multipliers (contact tractions); compared to the penalty method it usually leads to better conditioning and is less sensitive to the magnitude of the contact stiffness, but may require additional iterations especially if the deformed mesh becomes excessively distorted.
dFacts.note: Same claim as G3 (AugLag iterative penalty updates, better conditioning, less sensitive to stiffness, extra iterations with distorted mesh); verified at TR 22057-22061 but excluded as duplicate of G3.

dFacts.statement: For real constants FKN, FTOLN, PINB, PZER, CZER, FKOP, FKT, SLTO, TNOP, FDMN, and FDMT, the program interprets a positive value as a scaling factor and a negative value as the absolute value; the depth of the underlying element is the reference for FTOLN, PINB, and CZER.
dFacts.note: Lines 2509-2513 exact: FKN, FTOLN, PINB, PZER, CZER, FKOP, FKT, SLTO, TNOP, FDMN, FDMT positive=scaling factor, negative=absolute; underlying element depth is reference for FTOLN, PINB, CZER.

dFacts.statement: FKN = 10 for bonded; for all other contact behaviors FKN = 1.0, but if bonded and other contact behavior exist, FKN = 1 for all.
dFacts.note: Lines 2491-2492 exact: FKN=10 for bonded; 1.0 otherwise; if bonded and other behavior exist, FKN=1 for all.

dFacts.statement: Use a positive value of FDMN to specify a damping scaling factor in the normal direction (FDMN defaults to 1.0), and a positive value of FDMT for the tangential direction (FDMT defaults to 1.e-3); a negative value inputs an absolute tangential damping coefficient.
dFacts.note: Lines 4958-4963: positive FDMN = normal damping scaling factor (default 1.0); positive FDMT = tangential scaling factor (default 1.e-3); negative FDMT = absolute tangential damping coefficient. All sub-claims supported.

dFacts.statement: By setting the double-sided target surface option (KEYOPT(8)=1 of the TARGE170 target element), you can model double-sided contact pairs with only one set of the target surface; this option is only valid for 3D models with surface-to-surface (CONTA174) and node-to-surface (CONTA175) contacts.
dFacts.note: Lines 1758-1769 exact: TARGE170 KEYOPT(8)=1 double-sided target; only valid for 3D S-S (CONTA174) and node-to-surface (CONTA175).

dFacts.statement: You must use a pilot node in certain situations to control the boundary conditions and motion of the entire target surface, such as when the target is subjected to applied forces or rotations, is connected to other elements, or when modeling surface-based constraints or a rigid body.
dFacts.note: Lines 6042-6048 exact: pilot node required for applied forces, rotations, connection to other elements, surface-based constraints/rigid body.

dFacts.statement: By default KEYOPT(2)=0 for the target element and the program checks boundary conditions, treating target nodes along a DOF as fixed when there are no explicit BCs/prescribed forces, the nodes are not connected to other elements, and no CE/CP equations are used; KEYOPT(2)=1 lets you control the target node constraint conditions.
dFacts.note: Lines 6055-6066 exact: target KEYOPT(2)=0 default checks BCs (no explicit BCs/forces, no connected elements, no CE/CP -> treated fixed); KEYOPT(2)=1 user control.

dFacts.statement: For CONTA174 (also CONTA175 and CONTA177), real constant R1 is the radius if the target shape (TARGE170) is a cylinder, cone, or sphere, and R2 is the radius of a cone at the second node.
dFacts.note: Lines 1601-1604 exact: R1 = radius if TARGE170 cylinder/cone/sphere; R2 = radius of cone at second node (CONTA174/175/177).

dFacts.statement: If the target surface is flat (or nearly flat) you may select low-order target elements; if the target surface is curved you should select high-order target elements (set KEYOPT(1)=1 in the target element definition).
dFacts.note: Lines 1700-1703 exact: flat -> low-order target; curved -> high-order target (KEYOPT(1)=1).

dFacts.statement: In the basic Coulomb friction model, two contacting surfaces can carry shear stresses up to a certain magnitude (sticking); sliding begins when the equivalent shear stress Ï„ = Âµp + COHE is exceeded, where Âµ is the friction coefficient and COHE specifies cohesion sliding resistance.
dFacts.note: Lines 3489-3495 exact: Coulomb model, sticking up to equivalent shear stress tau = mu*p + COHE.

dFacts.statement: For frictionless, rough, and bonded contact the contact element stiffness matrices are symmetric, but contact problems involving friction produce unsymmetric stiffnesses; the program uses a symmetrization algorithm, and you can choose NROPT,UNSYM to improve convergence when frictional stresses are highly solution dependent.
dFacts.note: Statement at lines 3500-3507 (cited line 3499 is the preceding USERINTER sentence): symmetric stiffness for frictionless/rough/bonded, unsymmetric with friction, symmetrization algorithm, NROPT,UNSYM.

dFacts.statement: Isotropic friction (TB,FRIC,,,ISO) is available for 2D and 3D contact elements based on a single coefficient MU (TB command recommended or MP command); orthotropic friction is available only for the 3D contact elements (CONTA174, CONTA175, CONTA176, CONTA177) and uses two coefficients MU1 and MU2 with TB,FRIC,,,ORTHO / FORTHO / EORTHO options.
dFacts.note: Lines 3533-3560: isotropic (TB,FRIC,,,ISO) 2D/3D single MU (TB recommended or MP); orthotropic only 3D (CONTA174/175/176/177) with MU1/MU2 and ORTHO/FORTHO/EORTHO options.

dFacts.statement: CONTA174 supports isotropic and orthotropic Coulomb friction; for isotropic friction specify a single MU using TB (recommended) or MP, and for orthotropic friction specify two coefficients MU1 and MU2 in two principal directions using TB command input.
dFacts.note: Lines 34208-34211 exact: CONTA174 isotropic (single MU, TB recommended or MP) and orthotropic (MU1, MU2, TB) Coulomb friction.

dFacts.statement: TAUMAX is maximum contact friction with units of stress; regardless of the magnitude of normal contact pressure, sliding occurs if the friction stress reaches this value (used when contact pressure is very large such as in bulk metal forming); TAUMAX defaults to 1.0e20 and its value may be close to the yield stress Ïƒy of the material being deformed.
dFacts.note: Lines 3602-3609: TAUMAX max contact friction (stress units), sliding when friction stress reaches it, bulk metal forming use, default 1.0e20. Note: the formula after "close to" is missing in the extraction (blank at 3607); the sigma_y yield-stress relationship is supported by surrounding text.

dFacts.statement: Another real constant used for the friction law is the cohesion, COHE (default COHE=0), which has units of stress and provides sliding resistance even with zero normal pressure.
dFacts.note: Lines 3619-3621 exact: COHE default 0, stress units, sliding resistance with zero normal pressure.

dFacts.statement: FACT is the ratio of static to dynamic coefficients of friction and defaults to a minimum value of 1.0; DC is the decay coefficient (units time/length) and defaults to zero, in which case Âµ=MU for sliding and Âµ=FACT*MU for sticking.
dFacts.note: Statement at lines 3637-3641 (cited line 3635 is off): FACT ratio static/dynamic default min 1.0; DC decay coefficient time/length default 0; mu=MU sliding, mu=FACT*MU sticking.

dFacts.statement: Arctangent friction is designed to improve convergence by providing smoothly-varying frictional stress with respect to sliding velocity; unlike the Coulomb model it is viscous and its stiffness matrix is always unsymmetric, so you should activate the unsymmetric solver via NROPT,UNSYM; it is highly dependent on the reference slip rate v0.
dFacts.note: Lines 3728-3754: arctangent friction improves convergence, smoothly varying with sliding velocity, viscous, stiffness always unsymmetric -> NROPT,UNSYM, highly dependent on reference slip rate v0.

dFacts.statement: In a static analysis you can model steady-state frictional sliding between two flexible bodies (or a flexible and rigid body) with different predefined velocities via the CMROTATE command; this feature is applicable to 3D contact (CONTA174, CONTA175) and is primarily used for generating sliding contact at frictional interfaces in a brake squeal analysis.
dFacts.note: Lines 3655-3667 exact: steady-state frictional sliding via CMROTATE in static analysis; 3D contact CONTA174/CONTA175; brake squeal use.

dFacts.statement: Velocities defined by CMROTATE are ignored for frictionless contact, rough contact (KEYOPT(12)=1), bonded contact (KEYOPT(12)=3,5,6), and MPC contact (KEYOPT(2)=2).
dFacts.note: Lines 3672-3676 exact: CMROTATE velocities ignored for frictionless, rough (KEYOPT(12)=1), bonded (KEYOPT(12)=3,5,6), MPC (KEYOPT(2)=2).

dFacts.statement: Use real constant PINB to specify a scaling factor or absolute value for the pinball region; by default the program defines the pinball region as a circle for 2D or a sphere for 3D of radius 2*depth (rigid-to-flexible) or 1*depth (flexible-to-flexible) of the underlying element.
dFacts.note: Lines 4582-4587 exact: PINB scaling factor/absolute value; default circle(2D)/sphere(3D) radius 2*depth rigid-to-flexible, 1*depth flexible-to-flexible.

dFacts.statement: The nodal detection algorithms require the smoothing of the contact surface (KEYOPT(4)=1) or the smoothing of the target surface (KEYOPT(4)=2), which is time consuming and should be used only to deal with corner, point-to-surface, or edge-to-surface contact.
dFacts.note: Lines 3785-3787 exact: nodal detection requires smoothing (KEYOPT(4)=1 contact or =2 target), time consuming, only for corner/point-to-surface/edge-to-surface.

dFacts.statement: The dual shape function option is recommended for Lagrange multiplier contact (KEYOPT(2)=3 or 4), MPC bonded contact (KEYOPT(2)=2), and small sliding behavior (KEYOPT(18)=1 or 2).
dFacts.note: Lines 3885-3886 exact: dual shape function recommended for LM (KEYOPT(2)=3 or 4), MPC bonded (KEYOPT(2)=2), small sliding (KEYOPT(18)=1 or 2).

dFacts.statement: For Normal Lagrange formulation (KEYOPT(2)=3,4), with 3D higher-order contact elements (with midside nodes), use of surface projection-based contacts (KEYOPT(4)=3,4) is strongly recommended.
dFacts.note: Lines 3107-3109 exact: Normal Lagrange (KEYOPT(2)=3,4) + 3D higher-order (midside nodes) -> surface projection-based (KEYOPT(4)=3,4) strongly recommended.

dFacts.statement: The finite-sliding option is used by default (KEYOPT(18)=0) and allows arbitrary separation, sliding, and rotation; the small-sliding option (KEYOPT(18)=1) is appropriate when sliding motion is less than 20% of the contact length, and the adaptive small-sliding option (KEYOPT(18)=2) uses small sliding during a substep if the contact is closed at its beginning.
dFacts.note: Lines 3958-3998: finite sliding default KEYOPT(18)=0 (arbitrary separation/sliding/rotation); small sliding KEYOPT(18)=1 (<20% of contact length); adaptive KEYOPT(18)=2 (small sliding in substep if contact closed at its beginning).

dFacts.statement: CNCHECK,ADJUST physically moves contact nodes toward the target surface while leaving the rest of the model untouched; CNCHECK,MORPH moves contact nodes toward the target surface and also morphs the underlying solid element mesh to improve quality; CNCHECK,TADJUST moves the entire target body to engage the contact surface.
dFacts.note: ADJUST/MORPH exact at cited lines 4279-4283; TADJUST clause verified at line 4448 (SS3.9.11: "CNCHECK,TADJUST option moves the entire target body to engage with the contact surface"), outside the cited window but in the same guide.

dFacts.statement: Use real constant CNOF to specify a contact surface offset (positive toward the target, negative away), and set KEYOPT(5) as 1 (close gap), 2 (reduce initial penetration), or 3 (either).
dFacts.note: Cited line 4238 is in the STRM/TEND ramping text and does not support this. CNOF sign meaning exact at lines 4060-4062 (positive toward target, negative away); KEYOPT(5)=1 close gap / 2 reduce penetration / 3 either at lines 4076-4078 (SS3.9.8). True location: 4060.

dFacts.statement: You should always issue the CNCHECK command before starting the solution to verify the initial contact status.
dFacts.note: Cited line 4238 does not support this. Exact at lines 4042-4048: "you should always issue the CNCHECK command before starting the solution to verify the initial contact status." True location: 4042.

dFacts.statement: For standard contact (KEYOPT(12)=0) or rough contact (KEYOPT(12)=1), you can use real constants FDMN and FDMT to define contact damping scaling factors along contact normal and tangential directions; contact stabilization damping is deactivated by default and can be activated by setting KEYOPT(15)=2 or 3.
dFacts.note: Lines 4918-4922 (FDMN/FDMT for standard/rough), 4945 (deactivated by default), 4955-4956 (manually activate with KEYOPT(15)=2 or 3). All in cited window.

dFacts.statement: You can account for the thickness of shells (2D and 3D) and beams using KEYOPT(11); by default the program does not account for the element thickness, and beams/shells are discretized at their mid-surface in which penetration distance is calculated from the mid-surface.
dFacts.note: Cited line 11440 is in the node-to-node solution-options section (no KEYOPT(11)). Exact at lines 5064-5071 (SS3.9.20.1): KEYOPT(11) thickness for shells (2D/3D) and beams; default no thickness, mid-surface discretization, penetration from mid-surface. True location: 5065.

dFacts.statement: Use KEYOPT(7)=0,1,2, or 3 to control time stepping, where KEYOPT(7)=0 provides no control (the default) and KEYOPT(7)=3 provides the most control; KEYOPT(7)=4 activates impact constraints in a transient dynamic analysis with automatic adjustment of the time increment.
dFacts.note: Lines 5118-5132 exact: KEYOPT(7)=0 no control (default), 3 most control, 4 impact constraints in transient dynamic with automatic time increment adjustment.

dFacts.statement: The time step size must be small enough to capture the proper contact zone; a reliable way to set an accurate time step size is to turn automatic time stepping on (AUTOTS,ON), and you should use NROPT,FULL,,OFF and not adaptive descent; set NROPT,UNSYM when frictional sliding dominates; use NEQIT (defaults 15-26) and LNSRCH.
dFacts.note: Lines 6408-6430 exact: time step small enough for contact zone; AUTOTS,ON; NROPT,FULL,,OFF, no adaptive descent; NROPT,UNSYM when frictional sliding dominates; NEQIT default 15-26; LNSRCH.

dFacts.statement: You should avoid midside-noded elements for 3D contact surfaces when using the node-to-surface element CONTA175.
dFacts.note: Lines 1409-1411 exact: avoid midside-noded elements for 3D contact surfaces with CONTA175.

dFacts.statement: In general, if the underlying solid element has material properties defined by both TB and MP commands, the properties defined by TB take precedence over the properties defined by MP in the calculation of initial contact stiffness.
dFacts.note: Cited line 4238 does not support this. Exact at lines 3293-3295 (SS3.9.4.4): TB properties take precedence over MP in initial contact stiffness calculation. True location: 3293.

dFacts.statement: Ansys recommends using automatic generation (ESURF) for contact elements; this approach is simpler and more reliable.
dFacts.note: Lines 1854-1856: Ansys recommends automatic generation, simpler and more reliable; step 2 at line 1862 names the ESURF command.

dFacts.statement: You can check the direction of the outward normals for the contact elements with the /PSYMB,ESYS command; if the contact surface's outward normal does not point toward the target surface, reverse the node number order with ESURF,,REVE or reorient the element normals with ENORM.
dFacts.note: Lines 1873-1891: /PSYMB,ESYS check of outward normals; normal should point toward target; otherwise ESURF,,REVE or ENORM. Cited line 1890 inside the passage.

dFacts.statement: The pair-based contact definition is usually more efficient and more robust than the general contact definition; it supports more options and specific contact features.
dFacts.note: Lines 34153-34154 exact: pair-based usually more efficient and robust, supports more options and specific features.

dFacts.statement: Most contact models can employ either the pair-based contact method or the general contact method; the choice is a trade-off between ease of defining contact and solution robustness and performance, and general contact is mainly useful for models in which determining contact pairs between many parts is difficult or impossible.
dFacts.note: Lines 791-801 exact: either method possible; trade-off between ease of definition and robustness/performance; general contact mainly for many-part models where pairs are hard/impossible.

dFacts.statement: Features not supported by general contact include: Debonding and cohesive contact behavior (TB,CZM), Contact surface wear (TB,WEAR), Impact constraints (KEYOPT(7)=4), Brake squeal analysis (CMROTATE), and Fluid pressure penetration loading.
dFacts.note: Lines 845-850: list of features not available in general contact includes TB,CZM, TB,WEAR, impact constraints (KEYOPT(7)=4), brake squeal (CMROTATE), fluid pressure penetration (plus 4 more items not in the statement).

dFacts.statement: The general contact surfaces are formed automatically (GCGEN command) based on physical parts and geometric shapes; general contact fully identifies all possible contact (including self-contact) and minimizes user intervention.
dFacts.note: Lines 769-771 exact: general contact surfaces formed automatically (GCGEN) from parts/shapes; identifies all possible contact incl. self-contact; minimizes user intervention.

dFacts.statement: In a 3D general contact definition, the surface-to-surface contact formulation (CONTA174) may be combined with the 3D edge-to-surface formulation (CONTA177) and the 3D vertex-to-surface formulation CONTA175; CONTA174 is used as the primary contact constraint and CONTA177 and CONTA175 as supplemental constraints.
dFacts.note: Lines 782-785 exact: 3D general contact combines CONTA174 (primary) with CONTA177 and CONTA175 (supplemental).

dFacts.statement: The material ID and real constant ID input on GCDEF identify interface properties (defined by MP or TB commands) and contact control parameters (defined by the R command) for a specific contact interaction.
dFacts.note: Lines 34193-34195 exact: GCDEF material/real constant IDs identify MP/TB interface properties and R command control parameters.

dFacts.statement: For general contact, the GCGEN command automatically sets KEYOPT(2)=1 (penalty function).
dFacts.note: Note at lines 34390-34392 (cited line 34389 is the preceding KEYOPT(2)=4 line): GCGEN automatically sets KEYOPT(2)=1 (penalty) for general contact.

dFacts.statement: The default contact algorithm for pair-based APDL is Aug. Lagr. (Augmented Lagrangian); for general contact (GCGEN) it is Penalty.
dFacts.note: Cited line 2841 is a garbled multi-column table (columns Contact Wizard/Ansys Mechanical/APDL) in which the Aug. Lagr./Penalty values cannot be reliably attributed. The claim is clearly supported by the SS1.2.2 Difference in Default Settings table, lines 811-822: General Contact Default = Penalty method, Pair-Based Contact Default = Augmented Lagrange method. True location: 820.

dFacts.statement: Use real constant CNOF to specify a contact surface offset; set a positive value to offset the entire contact surface toward the target surface and a negative value away from it.
dFacts.note: Cited line 4238 does not support this. Exact at lines 4060-4062: positive CNOF offsets toward target, negative away. True location: 4060.

dFacts.statement: Mechanical APDL offers approaches to solve large initial penetrations gradually, including contact surface offset (CNOF) as a function of time via tabular input, ramping the penetration (KEYOPT(9)=2 or 4), and ramping the contact stiffness (KEYOPT(9)=2 or 4 with STRM/TEND); the initial interference fit is usually solved under frictionless conditions before applying all external loads.
dFacts.note: SS3.9.9 (lines 4178-4254) supports all sub-claims: method 1 CNOF vs time via tabular input (4179-4187); method 2 ramp penetration KEYOPT(9)=2 or 4 (4188-4189, 4251); method 3 stiffness ramping STRM/TEND (4223-4238, cited line inside); interference fit solved frictionless before external loads (4244-4245). Full list starts at 4178.

dFacts.statement: It is highly recommended that you apply the contact surface to the bolt and the target surface to the bolt hole, and symmetric contact should not be used for bolt thread modeling.
dFacts.note: Lines 2029-2033 exact: contact surface on bolt / target on bolt hole highly recommended; symmetric contact should not be used for bolt thread modeling.

dFacts.statement: Contact elements CONTA172, CONTA174, and CONTA177 support contact pair-splitting.
dFacts.note: Line 6475 exact: CONTA172, CONTA174, CONTA177 support contact pair-splitting.

dFacts.note: Lines 1908-1935: SECTYPE,SECID,CONTACT,CIRCLE/SPHERE/CYLINDER with SECDATA; applied via section ID (SECNUM/EMODIF).

dFacts.statement: Debonding refers to separation of bonded contact (KEYOPT(12)=2,3,4,5 or 6), is activated by associating a cohesive zone material model (TB,CZM) with contact elements, and is available only for pure penalty and augmented Lagrangian methods (KEYOPT(2)=0,1) with contact elements CONTA172, CONTA174, CONTA175, and CONTA177.
dFacts.note: Lines 22203-22206 exact: debonding = separation of bonded (KEYOPT(12)=2..6), TB,CZM, only penalty/AugLag (KEYOPT(2)=0,1), CONTA172/174/175/177.

dFacts.statement: Impact constraints can be selected by setting KEYOPT(7)=4 for any of the 2D or 3D contact elements and are valid for all types of contact interactions (flexible-to-flexible, flexible-to-rigid, and rigid-to-rigid) with and without friction; an automatic time stepping scheme is used to predict the time of impact.
dFacts.note: Lines 22133-22137 exact: KEYOPT(7)=4 for any 2D/3D contact element; all interaction types with/without friction; automatic time stepping predicts time of impact.

dFacts.statement: The contact damping coefficient is specified as a function of the opening gap based on upinb (pinball radius, real constant PINB), dn0 (normal contact damping coefficient, real constant FDMN), and dt0 (tangential contact damping coefficient, real constant FDMT).
dFacts.note: Cited line 21866 is in the friction-integration text and does not support this. Exact at lines 22108-22119 (SS13.174.5 Viscous Damping): damping coefficient specified as function of opening gap; upinb=PINB, dn0=FDMN, dt0=FDMT. True location: 22108.

dFacts.statement: The augmented Lagrange algorithm is used for the frictional contact pairs (brake squeal), as the pressure and frictional stresses are augmented during equilibrium iterations so penetration is reduced gradually; it requires fewer computational resources than the standard Lagrange multiplier algorithm and is well suited for general frictional contact.
dFacts.note: Lines 4991-4996 exact (brake squeal chapter): AugLag for frictional pairs, augmented during equilibrium iterations, fewer computational resources than standard LM, well suited for general frictional contact. Distinct from G3 (application + LM comparison claim).

dFacts.statement: An internal multipoint constraint (MPC) contact algorithm is used for bonded contact because it ties the contact and target surfaces together efficiently for solid-solid assembly, building equations internally based on contact kinematics and not requiring the DOF of the contact surface nodes; a contact detection point is made on the Gauss point for frictional pairs and on the nodal point (normal-to-target surface) for MPC bonded pairs.
dFacts.note: Lines 4997-5002 exact: MPC for bonded contact, ties surfaces efficiently, internal equations from contact kinematics, no contact-node DOF needed; Gauss-point detection for frictional pairs, nodal (normal-to-target) for MPC bonded.

dFacts.statement: The CMROTATE command defines constant rotational velocities on the contact/target nodes to generate a sliding frictional force in the brake squeal analysis (e.g., CMROTATE, E_ROTOR, , , 2).
dFacts.note: Lines 5007-5018: CMROTATE defines constant rotational velocities on contact/target nodes; E_ROTOR component specified in CMROTATE to generate sliding frictional force. Literal command "CMROTATE, E_ROTOR, , , 2" verified at line 5090 (same section).

dFacts.note: Lines 2759-2771 exact: standard S-S pair with augmented Lagrangian between cam and valve ball; CONTA174 + TARGE170; status changes during analysis.

dFacts.note: Lines 15751-15773 exact: et,2,CONTA174 + KEYOPT,2,10,2 (stiffness update each iteration) + et,3,TARGE170; tshap,cyli roller, r,3,1 radius 1; tshap,pilot node.

dFacts.note: Statement at lines 16280-16281 (cited line 16270 is off): variable coefficient of friction (0.4 to 0.2) via TB,FRIC with TBTEMP and TBDATA.

grid.statement: fedoo.constitutivelaw.ElastoPlasticity(young_modulus, poisson_ratio, yield_stress, name='') is a J2 elasto-plastic constitutive law with isotropic hardening (local return mapping, n_statev=7, statev = [P, EP(6)]); hardening is defined via set_hardening_function(function_type, **kwargs)
ElastoPlasticity does NOT implement the plane-stress ('2Dstress') return mapping; for plane-stress models use a Simcoon plasticity law, e.g. fedoo.constitutivelaw.Simcoon("EPICP", props)
fedoo.constitutivelaw.Simcoon("EPICP", props) with props = np.array([E, nu, alpha, Re, k, m]) gives isotropic plasticity with power law hardening sigma = k*eps_p**m

Standard workflow: fd.ModelingSpace("2Dplane"); mesh = fd.mesh.rectangle_mesh(nx=41, ny=21, x_min=0, x_max=L, y_min=0, y_max=h, elm_type="quad4", name="Domain"); wf = fd.weakform.StressEquilibrium("ConstitutiveLaw", nlgeom=False); fd.Assembly.create(wf, "Domain", "quad4", name="Assembling"); pb = fd.problem.NonLinear("Assembling")

The incremental nonlinear solve is driven by pb.nlsolve(dt=0.05, tmax=1, update_dt=False, tol_nr=0.05, interval_output=0.05), or by a manual Newton-Raphson loop: pb.assembly.set_start(pb), pb.apply_boundary_conditions(t_fact, t_fact_old), pb.set_A(pb.assembly.get_global_matrix()), pb.set_D(pb.assembly.get_global_vector()), pb.solve(), then pb.assembly.update(pb) in sub-iterations until norm_res < tol_nr

Boundary conditions: pb.bc.add("Dirichlet", nodes, "Disp", 0) / pb.bc.add("Dirichlet", nodes, "DispY", uimp); outputs: pb.add_output(path, "Assembling", ["Disp", "Stress", "Strain", "Statev", "Wm"], output_type="Node", file_format="vtk")

grid.statement: fd.weakform.StressEquilibrium(constitutivelaw, incompressibility=None, convert_tangent=True, name="", nlgeom=None, space=None) is the mechanical equilibrium weak form, usable for 3D solids or 2D plane assumptions (plane strain / plane stress)

nlgeom parameter: False = ignore geometric nonlinearities; True or 'UL' = updated Lagrangian method (mesh is updated); 'TL' = total Lagrangian method; if not defined, the problem.nlgeom parameter is used (used in NonLinearStatic / NonLinearNewmark problems)
The incompressibility attribute selects the method used to avoid volumetric locking of nearly incompressible materials; by default (None) the standard displacement formulation is used

The weak form creates the DOF vector "Disp" (DispX, DispY, and DispZ in 3D), tags second-order time evolution, and the corate attribute selects the corotational formulation (default 'log_r', other options 'log', 'jaumann', 'gn'...)
fd.mesh.rectangle_mesh(nx=11, ny=11, x_min=0, x_max=1, y_min=0, y_max=1, elm_type='quad4', ndim=None, name='') creates a rectangular mesh; elm_type in {'tri3','tri6','quad4','quad8','quad9'}

Other mesh builders exist: box_mesh (3D volume mesh, simple.py line 478) and disk_mesh(radius, nr, nt, elm_type='quad4') (structured_mesh.py line 408); modeling spaces are set with fd.ModelingSpace("2Dplane") or "3D"
